newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistani stocks soar on Bhutto's dismissal.
newsitem.headline: Pakistani stocks soar on Bhutto's dismissal.

text.p: Pakistani stocks notched their biggest gains of the year on Wednesday and the local currency was expected to strengthen in reaction to the sacking of Benazir Bhutto's government, dealers said.
Karachi's 100-share index surged nearly 110 points to 1,607.84 before profit-taking kicked in later in the session. It closed 78.63 points or 5.25 percent higher at 1,577.40.
"The market over-reacted to the government's dismissal and profit-taking trimmed the early gains," said one dealer at the Karachi bourse. "But overall market sentiment is positive."
Some dealers said the index appeared poised for a sustained move above the 1,600 point level.
Currency dealers said the bullish tone in the Karachi exchange was expected to flow into the local currency market and prompt many investors to switch from dollars to rupees.
The rupee opened slightly lower at 43 to the dollar in the kerb market on Wednesday, but was expected to firm soon.
"There is a lot of dollar selling as people invest in stocks expected to gain after Bhutto's dismissal," one dealer said.
A local holiday prevented trading on Tuesday when President Farooq Leghari sacked Bhutto, dissolved parliament and named an interim prime minister to supervise elections set for February 3.
Leghari said Bhutto's government had to go because it was irretrievably tainted by corruption, nepotism and misrule.

Currency dealer Owais Kalia of Khanani and Kalia International said investors often sought a safe haven in the dollar in times of political or economic uncertainty, but hopes that Bhutto's departure was seen stabilising the rupee market.
The State (central) Bank of Pakistan rate was unchanged at 40.1200/40.3206 to the dollar, set on October 22.

Looking ahead, many Karachi analysts said the markets would look favourably on an anti-corruption drive by the new interim government led by Meraj Khalid, even if the time needed for this led to a postponement of promised elections.

They said investors and businessmen placed a higher priority on cleansing Pakistan's political and economic system than on holding quick elections that might simply return to power another set of politicians with dubious credentials.
The focus was firmly on politics as the markets believed the caretaker government would follow economic policy guidelines set by the International Monetary Fund, the analysts said.

"The president may ask the judiciary to extend the interim set-up indefinitely until the accountability process for the politicians is completed," analyst Alia Ehmar of ING Barings said in a research report.

Nauman Sheikh of KASB & Co said a strong democratic system could only be installed in Pakistan if effective mechanisms to stop corruption were put in place, a population census carried out and the rule of law firmly established.
"The market is concerned that if the same or a similar pack of people return to power in the February polls, the whole purpose of the president's exercise would be defeated," he said.
Pakistan held its last population count in 1981. The next should have been held in 1991, but successive governments postponed it for fear of possible political repercussions.
The population of the four provinces determines the number of seats they have in the National Assembly (lower house) as well as their share in federal resources and employment.

Ehmar said that extending the interim government's life could give a chance to third parties with clean records to put up a credible challenge to Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party and the main opposition Pakistan Muslim League of Nawaz Sharif.
However, some analysts said it might be dangerous to place total confidence in the ability of Leghari and the caretaker government to resist the temptations of office for too long.
